---
title: "Foundation Models and Emerging Directions"
---

This chapter surveys the current frontier of representation learning in biology. It
separates three kinds of statement: results that are reported and verifiable in the
primary literature, ambitions that are stated as programs rather than achieved
outcomes, and outright speculation about where the field is heading. Whenever the
text moves from the first category to the others, it says so. The examples span
nucleotide, protein, structure, single-cell, molecular, and image modalities, and
each is described only at the level of detail its primary source supports.

## What "Foundation Model" Means in Biology

::: {.callout-note}
## Definition

A **foundation model** is a model trained on broad data at scale, usually with a
self-supervised objective, that produces representations or capabilities
transferable to many downstream tasks through adaptation (fine-tuning, prompting,
or linear probing) rather than task-specific training from scratch
[@bommasani2021opportunities]. In this book the term is used more narrowly: a model
pretrained on a large unlabelled corpus of a single biological modality, whose
**embeddings** serve as reusable features.

:::

The recipe crystallized in natural language processing, where masked-language-model
pretraining followed by fine-tuning replaced per-task feature engineering
[@devlin2019bert]. Biology adopted the same pattern because its data have a
convenient property: unlabelled sequences, structures, and expression matrices are
abundant, while labels are scarce. A foundation model therefore front-loads the
expensive learning into an unlabelled pretraining stage and amortizes it across many
small labeled tasks.

Three properties distinguish a foundation model from the classical embeddings of
earlier chapters. First, **scale** in parameters and data. Second, **generality**:
one checkpoint feeds classification, regression, generation, and retrieval. Third,
**adaptation**: the embedding is consumed by a lightweight head, so the cost of
entering a new task is small. A model that is large but trained for exactly one task
is not a foundation model in this sense.

Adaptation is what makes the pretraining cost worth paying, and it can be stated
formally. Fix the pretrained encoder $f_\theta:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}$, mapping
an entity $e\in\mathcal{X}$ (here a sequence) to its embedding
$f_\theta(e)=\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$, and freeze $\theta$. A linear probe adds
parameters $\mathbf{w}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ and $b\in\mathbb{R}$ and minimizes

$$
\min_{\mathbf{w},\,b}\ \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\ell\!\left(\hat y_i,\,y_i\right),
\qquad
\hat y_i =
\begin{cases}
\sigma\!\left(\mathbf{w}^{\top}\mathbf{x}_i+b\right), & \text{classification},\\[2pt]
\mathbf{w}^{\top}\mathbf{x}_i+b, & \text{regression},
\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-ch13-probe}

over a labelled set $\{(e_i,y_i)\}_{i=1}^{n}$, where $y_i$ is the task label, $\ell$
is a per-example loss (cross-entropy for classification, squared error for
regression), and $\sigma$ is the logistic sigmoid applied for the classification
link (regression uses the identity). Only $d+1$ parameters are fit, which is why the probe is
the cheapest test of whether a frozen embedding carries task-relevant information;
for the losses and links used here the objective @eq-ch13-probe is convex, so it has no
spurious local minima.

The dominant pretraining objective differs by modality because the data differ.
Nucleotide and amino-acid language models overwhelmingly use masked or denoising
objectives inherited from BERT [@devlin2019bert], which suit fixed-length sequences
and yield bidirectional context. Generative models instead use autoregressive
objectives: ProGen models protein sequences left to right [@madani2023large], and a
decoder-only architecture can do the same for general protein design
[@ferruz2022protgpt2], while Evo applies a causal, long-context objective across
nucleotide and protein tokens [@nguyen2024sequence]. Contrastive objectives, which
need paired views of the same entity, dominate cross-modal alignment rather than
single-modality pretraining [@radford2021learning]. The choice is not cosmetic: an
encoder captures bidirectional evidence for a score, whereas an autoregressive model
can also sample new sequences, which is why design applications tend to build on the
latter.

Both objectives are per-token cross-entropies (Appendix A) and differ only in which
positions condition each prediction. Let $x=(x_1,\dots,x_T)$ be a token sequence
drawn from an alphabet $\mathcal{V}$, with $x_i\in\mathcal{V}$, and let
$M\subseteq\{1,\dots,T\}$ be a random set of masked positions. Masked pretraining
minimizes

$$
L_{\mathrm{MLM}}(\theta)=-\,\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}\,
\mathbb{E}_{M}\sum_{i\in M}\log p_\theta\!\left(x_i \mid x_{\setminus M}\right)
$$ {#eq-ch13-mlm}

where $\mathcal{D}$ is the pretraining corpus and $x_{\setminus M}$ is $x$ with the
tokens in $M$ replaced by a mask symbol; the sum runs over masked positions only, so
each term is the negative log-likelihood the model assigns to a masked token given
its visible context. An autoregressive (causal) model instead factorizes the joint
distribution left to right and minimizes

$$
L_{\mathrm{AR}}(\theta)=-\,\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}\sum_{t=1}^{T}
\log p_\theta\!\left(x_t \mid x_{<t}\right),
$$ {#eq-ch13-ar}

where $x_{<t}=(x_1,\dots,x_{t-1})$. The masked objective @eq-ch13-mlm lets every position
depend on both directions and is preferred when the representation feeds a scoring
head, whereas the causal objective @eq-ch13-ar additionally defines a normalized
distribution over sequences, which is what allows an autoregressive model to sample
novel sequences [@madani2023large; @ferruz2022protgpt2].

## Scaling Laws and What Transfers

Scaling laws quantify how test loss falls as a power law in model size, dataset
size, and compute for language models [@kaplan2020scaling], and specify the
compute-optimal trade-off between the two that later work revised toward
data-heavy training [@hoffmann2022training]. These empirical laws are the economic
argument for pretraining at scale: below the compute budget, larger and more
data-hungry models buy predictable gains.

To make this precise, let $N$ be the number of non-embedding model parameters, $D$
the number of training tokens, and $L$ the test loss (per-token cross-entropy, in
nats). Kaplan et al. reported that this loss falls as a power law in the number of
non-embedding parameters [@kaplan2020scaling]; adding an irreducible-loss floor
$L_\infty$, as in Hoffmann et al. [@hoffmann2022training], gives the functional form

$$
L(N)=L_\infty+\left(\frac{N_c}{N}\right)^{\alpha_N},
$$ {#eq-ch13-scaling-law}

with $L_\infty\ge 0$ an irreducible loss floor, $N_c>0$ a characteristic parameter
scale, and $\alpha_N>0$ the scaling exponent. The "power law" name comes from the fit
used to estimate $\alpha_N$: subtracting the floor and taking logarithms gives

$$
\log\bigl(L(N)-L_\infty\bigr)=\alpha_N\log N_c-\alpha_N\log N,
$$ {#eq-ch13-scaling-fit}

so $\alpha_N$ is recovered as the negative slope of a straight-line regression of
$\log(L-L_\infty)$ on $\log N$ (the fit @eq-ch13-scaling-fit) [@kaplan2020scaling]. The loss therefore falls
predictably with scale, but the exponent is an empirical constant particular to a
corpus and architecture: nothing in @eq-ch13-scaling-law forces the value found for
natural language to hold for a nucleotide or protein corpus.

Training compute enters through the same accounting. For a dense transformer, compute
is dominated by matrix multiplies, and one forward pass over $D$ tokens with $N$
parameters costs about $2ND$ floating-point operations, with the backward pass adding
roughly twice that, so the total training budget is approximately

$$
C \approx 6ND \quad\text{FLOPs}.
$$ {#eq-ch13-compute}

Given a fixed budget $C$, the compute-optimal allocation minimizes the loss subject
to @eq-ch13-compute:

$$
(N^\star,D^\star)=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{N,\,D\,:\,6ND\le C} L(N,D).
$$ {#eq-ch13-compute-optimal}

Hoffmann et al. reported that $N^\star\propto C^{a}$ and $D^\star\propto C^{b}$ with
$a+b=1$ and $a\approx b\approx 0.5$ — model size and data volume growing in equal
proportion with compute — revising the earlier Kaplan allocation, which favoured
larger models relative to data [@kaplan2020scaling; @hoffmann2022training]. Because
@eq-ch13-scaling-law and @eq-ch13-compute-optimal were fitted to language corpora, using them
to justify a particular biological model size is an extrapolation, not a guarantee.

Proteins provided the clearest biological analogue. Scaling unsupervised training to
250 million sequences produced ESM-1b, whose representations expose structure and
function without supervision [@rives2021biological]. Scaling further to 15 billion
parameters in ESM-2 was reported to improve structure prediction and variant-effect
signals and has produced widely reused protein embeddings [@lin2023evolutionary].
Protein-specific scaling behavior has been reported over several orders of
magnitude, but the exponents are not guaranteed to match those of natural language.
Whether language scaling laws transfer quantitatively to nucleotide, single-cell, or
molecular corpora remains an open empirical question; statements to the contrary
should be treated with caution.

Two cautions follow. First, lower pretraining loss does not guarantee better
downstream performance: the relationship between the training objective and an
arbitrary task is indirect, and gains often saturate for tasks far from pretraining.
Second, scaling laws estimate loss, not the properties a practitioner cares about —
calibration, robustness to distribution shift, or behavior on rare families.
Reported scaling of protein language models therefore motivates larger models but
does not by itself establish that they are more useful for any specific application.

## Modality-Specific Foundation Models: A Comparison

Every major biological modality now has at least one pretrained sequence or graph
model. For DNA, DNABERT applied k-mer tokenization and masked language modeling to
genomic sequence [@ji2021dnabert]; DNABERT-2 replaced k-mers with byte-pair encoding
and multi-species pretraining [@zhou2024dnabert2]; the Nucleotide Transformer
trained masked encoders on thousands of human and multi-species genomes for
regulatory tasks [@dallatorre2024nucleotide]; HyenaDNA used a state-space backbone
to reach nucleotide-resolution contexts up to very long windows
[@nguyen2023hyenadna]; and Evo scaled a hybrid architecture to genome length for
both prediction and design [@nguyen2024sequence].

For proteins, ESM-2 [@lin2023evolutionary] shares the modality with ProtT5
[@elnaggar2022prottrans] and the original ESM-1b [@rives2021biological]. Protein
*structure* has its own line of models: AlphaFold2 predicts coordinates from
multiple sequence alignments [@jumper2021highly], OpenFold retrains it openly to
study generalization and efficiency [@ahdritz2024openfold], and inverse-folding
models such as ESM-IF predict sequence from backbone [@hsu2022learning].

Single-cell data produced a distinct family: scBERT applied tokenized gene
expression with a BERT-style objective [@yang2022scbert], Geneformer pretrained on
ranked gene tokens for transfer across network-biology tasks
[@theodoris2023transfer], scGPT generalizes a generative transformer across
single-cell multi-omics [@cui2024scgpt], and scFoundation scales a masked model to
tens of millions of cells [@hao2024large]. Molecules have MolFormer, a
SMILES-based chemical language model [@ross2022large], alongside the supervised
message-passing baseline Chemprop [@yang2019analyzing]. Pathology contributed
vision-language models that jointly embed images and text [@lu2024visual].

The pattern across modalities is consistent: a tokenization choice (k-mers, byte-pair
encoding, single nucleotides, ranked genes, or SMILES atoms), a pretraining objective
(masked or causal), and an adaptation recipe (linear probe or fine-tune). What differs
is the inductive bias each modality requires. DNA is double-stranded and
reverse-complement-symmetric; proteins carry strong evolutionary signal encoded in
covariation; single-cell matrices are sparse counts with a dominant technical axis
(library size); molecules have explicit graph structure. Designs that respect the relevant symmetry are motivated by this sample-efficiency
argument, which is why structure- and symmetry-aware models persist alongside purely
sequence-based ones [@hsu2022learning; @dauparas2022robust]; the size of the effect is
task-dependent and is not quantified here.

Table 13.1 summarizes the landscape. Scales are those reported in the cited primary
source and are given only where the primary source states them.

| Model | Modality | Pretraining objective | Reported scale | Representative use | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ESM-2 | Protein sequence | Masked language model | up to 15B params | Structure, variant effects, embeddings | [@lin2023evolutionary] |
| ESM-1b | Protein sequence | Masked language model | — | General protein embeddings | [@rives2021biological] |
| ProtT5 | Protein sequence | Span denoising | — | Per-residue embeddings | [@elnaggar2022prottrans] |
| AlphaFold2 | Structure (MSA) | Supervised structure | — | Structure prediction | [@jumper2021highly] |
| OpenFold | Structure (MSA) | Supervised (reimplementation) | — | Reproducible structure prediction | [@ahdritz2024openfold] |
| ESM-IF | Structure | Inverse folding | — | Sequence design from backbone | [@hsu2022learning] |
| DNABERT-2 | DNA | Masked LM, BPE tokens | 117M params | Multi-species genome tasks | [@zhou2024dnabert2] |
| Nucleotide Transformer | DNA | Masked language model | up to 2.5B params | Regulatory genomics | [@dallatorre2024nucleotide] |
| HyenaDNA | DNA | Causal LM (state space) | — | Long-context genome modeling | [@nguyen2023hyenadna] |
| Evo | DNA + protein | Causal LM (hybrid) | 7B params | Genome-scale prediction and design | [@nguyen2024sequence] |
| scBERT | scRNA-seq | Masked gene LM | — | Cell-type annotation | [@yang2022scbert] |

## Multimodal and Generalist Models; the Virtual Cell

Contrastive image-text alignment demonstrated that two modalities can share one
embedding space in which retrieval and zero-shot classification work
[@radford2021learning]; pathology vision-language models apply the same idea to
histology and reports [@lu2024visual]. Within structural biology, the coupling runs
in both directions: sequence embeddings drive structure prediction
[@lin2023evolutionary; @jumper2021highly], and backbone-conditioned inverse folding
maps structure back to sequence [@hsu2022learning]. Sequence–structure alignment of
this kind is the most mature multimodal case in the book.

The more ambitious target is a **virtual cell**: a model that predicts cellular
state and its response to perturbation across modalities, contexts, and scales
[@bunne2024how]. That paper is explicit that this is a research program with
priorities and open problems, not a solved system. It is important not to read the
existing single-cell foundation models [@cui2024scgpt; @hao2024large] as already
constituting a virtual cell. Measured against the definition, they provide reusable
cell embeddings but do not yet predict arbitrary perturbations across modalities
with calibrated uncertainty. The distance between current models and the stated
goal is the honest summary; bridging it is an aspiration, not a reported result. The
priorities that paper lists — data generation across scales, benchmarks that respect
biological structure, and calibrated uncertainty — map directly onto the challenge
table below.

## Agentic and Reasoning Systems over Biological Embeddings

A newer direction uses large language models as controllers that call scientific
tools, read results, and iterate. An autonomous chemical-research system that
plans and executes experiments with laboratory hardware demonstrates the pattern in
a controlled setting [@boiko2023autonomous]. In the embedding-centric view of this
book, such agents sit one layer above the representations: embeddings supply a
retrieval and scoring substrate — nearest neighbors in sequence space, candidate
molecules ranked by a learned property model, structures scored by a folding model
— and the agent sequences calls to those scorers.

This area is early and should be read as such. Reported agentic results are
narrow, are often bounded by the tools available to the agent, and inherit every
evaluation weakness of the underlying embedding models discussed in Chapter 11.
Claims that agents "do biology" autonomously currently outrun the evidence.

The plausible near-term role is narrower than the headline claim. Agents are useful
where a decision decomposes into retrievals and scorings that embeddings already
perform well — proposing candidates, filtering a library, or summarizing a screen —
and where a human remains responsible for the final call. Genuine autonomy requires
reliable tools, calibrated confidence, and error recovery, none of which current
embedding models provide on their own.

## Open Challenges

Five challenges recur across modalities. Table 13.2 states each challenge, the
concrete evidence, and the open question.

| Challenge | What it is | Evidence | Open question |
|---|---|---|---|
| Data curation | Heterogeneous, redundant, and unevenly annotated corpora | Protein and genomic pretraining corpora [@rives2021biological; @dallatorre2024nucleotide] | Provenance and metadata standards for pretraining data |
| Evaluation | Benchmark overfitting and leakage inflate reported gains | Task benchmarks and integration studies [@rao2019evaluating; @luecken2022benchmarking] | Held-out tests that respect homology and distribution shift |
| Compute | Pretraining cost, carbon, and access asymmetry | Scaling-law trade-offs [@kaplan2020scaling; @hoffmann2022training] | Efficient domain-specific models that rival general ones |
| Licensing | Unclear reuse terms for data and for released weights | Foundation-model risk analysis [@bommasani2021opportunities] | Consent-aware licensing for genomes and clinical data |
| Ethics | Privacy of human genomes; dual-use of design models | Foundation-model risk analysis [@bommasani2021opportunities] | Governance appropriate to generative biology |

Table 13.2: Challenges for biological foundation models.

Evaluation deserves emphasis because it is where foundation models are most often
oversold. Reported gains on a benchmark can reflect leakage of homologous sequences
between pretraining and test sets rather than genuine transfer
[@rao2019evaluating], and single-cell integration quality depends strongly on the
metric chosen [@luecken2022benchmarking]. A foundation model is only as credible as
the evaluation that isolates its contribution from these confounds.

Data curation is the least glamorous constraint and arguably the binding one.
Pretraining corpora are assembled from databases with different annotation
standards, contain near-duplicate sequences, and carry unknown provenance
[@rives2021biological; @dallatorre2024nucleotide]; models trained on them inherit
those defects and can reproduce them at scale. Compute access determines who can
pretrain: the compute-optimal frontier shifts cost between model size and data
volume [@hoffmann2022training], and only well-resourced groups can explore it.
Licensing compounds the problem, because released weights and the data behind them
often carry terms incompatible with clinical or commercial use, a risk emphasized in
the foundation-model literature [@bommasani2021opportunities]. Ethical concerns are
modality-specific: human genomes and clinical records raise privacy questions that
protein sequences do not, while generative protein and molecule models raise
dual-use questions.

## Speculative Outlook (Labelled as Speculation)

The remainder of this section is explicitly speculative; it is not supported by the
cited results and should be read as informed conjecture.

- **Unified biomolecular models.** A single model spanning nucleotide, protein, and
  small-molecule tokens may emerge as tokenization converges. Speculation: whether
  one architecture beats well-tuned specialists is unknown, and reported comparisons
  have tended to favour specialists so far.
- **Interactive, tool-using models.** Embedding models may be invoked by reasoning
  agents rather than queried directly by humans. Speculation: the division of labor
  between learned scorers and external tools is unsettled.
- **Simulation-adjacent virtual cells.** If perturbation prediction matures, cell
  models could serve as cheap surrogates for experiments. Speculation: calibration
  and out-of-distribution reliability are the barriers, not raw accuracy.

None of these should be presented as a current capability. Each is a hypothesis
about direction, and each could fail to materialize.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Key Takeaways

- A foundation model is pretrained at scale with self-supervision and adapted to
  many tasks; in biology it is usually modality-specific [@bommasani2021opportunities].
- Language scaling laws are empirical and may not transfer quantitatively to
  biological data; treat cross-domain extrapolation as an open question
  [@kaplan2020scaling; @hoffmann2022training].
- Every major modality now has reusable pretrained encoders: ESM-2 for proteins
  [@lin2023evolutionary], the Nucleotide Transformer and Evo for DNA
  [@dallatorre2024nucleotide; @nguyen2024sequence], scGPT and scFoundation for
  single cells [@cui2024scgpt; @hao2024large].
- The virtual cell is a stated program, not an achieved system [@bunne2024how];
  current cell models provide embeddings, not calibrated perturbation prediction.
- Data curation, evaluation leakage, compute access, licensing, and ethics are the
  binding practical limits, and evaluation is the most frequent source of
  overstated claims [@rao2019evaluating; @luecken2022benchmarking].
:::
